Patient Information
		Female, 15 years old.

		Present Illness:
		The patient reported that during childhood her parents often worked at construction sites and were rarely at home. She and her younger sibling mainly lived with their grandparents. She described a lack of effective communication with her parents and difficulty obtaining support when facing problems.

		She stated that in the fifth grade of primary school she experienced social exclusion by classmates, which led to low mood, sadness, crying, and self-harm by cutting her hand with a small knife. The episode was brief and remitted spontaneously. She did not disclose this to her family, and thus it did not receive attention.

		According to the patient, she performed well academically in primary school, consistently ranking among the top in her class. After entering middle school, her academic stress gradually increased, and her test rankings declined. She felt that her family frequently compared her to others, magnifying her shortcomings and failing to recognize her efforts.

		Two years ago, she began experiencing difficulty initiating sleep, excessive thoughts (mainly of negative events), unexplained crying, and nightmares. She would awaken feeling tense and was unable to resume sleep. Her total sleep time decreased, often limited to about four hours, sometimes experiencing complete insomnia. During the daytime she had difficulty concentrating in class, frequent mind-wandering, unexplained low mood, emotional instability, irritability, and anger outbursts leading to conflicts with others. She frequently used cutting her hands as a way to vent emotions and felt a sense of relief afterwards. She reported recurrent pessimistic and negative thoughts with repeated self-injurious behavior.

		After entering the third year of middle school, her symptoms did not improve. She continued to have recurrent negative thoughts, and her cutting behavior increased compared to the previous year. She frequently cried uncontrollably during class, felt unwilling to speak or interact with others, became easily irritated when spoken to, experienced unexplained staring spells, and lost interest in previously enjoyed activities. Although she occasionally went out with friends, she felt unable to integrate or experience happiness.

		She reported increased difficulty with learning and marked decline in memory. She developed unexplained tinnitus and occasional auditory experiences of hearing people’s voices, such as hearing someone call her name before falling asleep at night. In crowded places, she felt inexplicably tense and fearful, without understanding the reason. She believed that when others stared at her, they might have ill intentions or that their behaviors made her uncomfortable. She began avoiding crowded places. During holidays at home, she mostly stayed alone in her room. When her family asked questions, she would lose control of her emotions. Her academic performance was affected.

		She first visited our outpatient clinic on May 28, 2024 and was diagnosed with “depressive state.” She was prescribed sertraline hydrochloride 50 mg at night and quetiapine fumarate 25 mg at night. The medication enabled her to sleep reluctantly but with insufficient duration, and her mood improvement was unsatisfactory. She returned for multiple follow-up visits, and her medication was adjusted to sertraline hydrochloride 100 mg at night and quetiapine fumarate 0.05 g at night. Sleep improved compared to before, but mood improvement remained unsatisfactory.

		After entering high school successfully at the end of August this year, she perceived worsening symptoms over the past month. She reported almost no good sleep at night, inability to continue attending classes during the day, increasing academic underperformance compared to others, lack of recognition by her family, persistent self-blame and guilt, recurrent pessimistic thoughts, and increased self-cutting behavior (with deeper cuts). She felt that her family did not understand her sadness. Frequent communication difficulties led to conflicts with family, emotional instability, and loss of control. She felt that her sleep worsened despite medication and self-increased her nighttime dose of quetiapine fumarate to 0.1–0.2 g per night. While she was able to sleep, she still experienced frequent nightmares.

		Recently, during holidays at home, she frequently lost control of her emotions and repeatedly engaged in self-cutting. Yesterday, during a particularly low mood episode, she ingested 15 quetiapine fumarate tablets without serious consequences but continued to feel extremely pessimistic, expressing suicidal thoughts. She cut both forearms with a blade, refused food, and her weight changes were unclear. Her family, perceiving the severity of her condition, brought her to our hospital today. She was admitted voluntarily to our ward with the diagnosis of “depressive state.”

		Family History: Negative.

		Past History:
		She denied any history of epilepsy, asthma, diabetes, heart disease, glaucoma, or other somatic illnesses. She denied any history of hepatitis, tuberculosis, typhoid, or other acute or chronic infectious diseases. She denied any history of surgery, trauma, coma, or blood transfusion. She denied any drug or food allergies. She received routine immunizations according to the schedule.

		Physical Examination:
		General condition stable; vital signs within normal limits; no obvious positive findings on physical examination.

		Auxiliary Examinations: None remarkable.

		Mental Status Examination:
		The patient was conscious, with intact orientation and cooperative in contact. She was able to answer questions appropriately. Thought processes were slowed; speech was slow, with low volume and reduced quantity. She exhibited psychogenic verbal hallucinations and ideas of reference. Mood was depressed, with frequent crying during the interview, self-blame, guilt, and feelings of worthlessness. She reported recurrent negative thoughts and repeated self-cutting behavior. She had a history of one recent non-lethal overdose attempt. Her emotions were unstable, with irritability, episodic agitation, restlessness, and pacing. Her affect was congruent with her inner experience and the surrounding environment. She showed pathological volitional decline, decreased interest, low energy, spending more time in bed, social withdrawal, and refusal to communicate with her family. She avoided social interactions, struggled to continue studying, and her academic performance was affected. She had difficulty concentrating. Intellectual function appeared intact. Remote and recent memory were preserved, but immediate memory was slightly impaired. She reported sometimes forgetting what she had just said a moment earlier. She recognized that she was ill but lacked insight into her disease and related symptoms.

		Date of Admission: October 7, 2024.

Primary Diagnosis:
		F32.3 - Major depressive episode with psychotic features.

		Comorbid Psychiatric Diagnoses:
		Sleep disorder.
